The Chirps and the Welcome Tree

The Arrow That Danced

Chip had made a magnificent arrow. It was nearly as long as he was. He hung it at the fork where visitors would turn toward the birdhouse for Everybody Day.

Along came Toad. The arrow pointed toward the cabbages. “Lovely,” said Toad. “I have always wanted to go to a cabbage party.” Off he went.

Chip flew down. The arrow pointed at the birdhouse again. He put one eye very close. The arrow behaved beautifully. He put both eyes very close. Still beautiful.

Behind him Caty sneezed. The arrow swung round and tapped Chip on the beak. “Oh,” he said. From somewhere among the cabbages, Toad called, “Am I early?”

Chip turned the sign the right way. He tied its tail to the fence as well as hanging its middle on the peg. “Now give it your very biggest sneeze,” he told Caty.

But Caty couldn’t sneeze to order. She puffed. Bella flapped. Daisy fanned the sign with the invitation. The arrow trembled from nose to tail. Its nose kept pointing home.

Toad came back carrying one curly cabbage leaf like a party hat. This time he followed the arrow all the way to the crooked roof. “Much better company,” he decided.

On a paper leaf for the Welcome Tree, Chip drew the fork and his steady arrow. Down in the garden the arrow had a little wiggle in the wind. Chip thought it had earned a dance.

Read together

How could you test a sign on a windy day?
